stock.counterargument: The honest counterargument is the sample: this process has not been shown to work, and a single ranking position is not evidence about one company.
invalidation: Quarterly revenue growth falling below +47.8%, the rate it was running at the quarter before.
Cash conversion dropping below 1.0×, meaning earnings stop being backed by cash.
A close below the 200-session average, which stood at $55.29 on the decision date.
risks: The most recent filing covers a period ending 2026-10-30, 18 days before the decision date.
Point-in-time fundamentals are built from filings accepted up to 2026-11-17.

earnings.basis: the same fiscal quarter's announcement a year earlier (2026-02-27) plus 364 days

stock.rule: Universe: every US-listed common stock on NYSE, Nasdaq or NYSE American — about 4,700 names from Nasdaq Trader's own file. Eligible means: priced at $5 or more, median daily turnover of $20M or more over 60 sessions, at least 253 sessions of history, a 10-Q or 10-K whose period ended within 200 days, close above the 200-session average, volatility inside the day's 85th percentile, debt no more than 6× operating cash flow, no results announced in the last 2 sessions, and no position already open in the stock or a fourth in the same SIC division. Eligible candidates are then ranked on equally weighted z-scores within their sector group, over the signals that are defined for that group. One position per session, held 21 sessions, a twenty-first of capital each, 10 basis points of cost each way. Fundamentals are read as they stood on the decision date, never as they read today. The score is a ranking position among that day's eligible candidates. It is not a probability, a price target, or a forecast of any return.
stock.validation: The held-out window has not been opened. No claim of an edge is made or implied.

stories.title: How the East Potomac golf course became a D.C. landmark — and what could happen to it
stories.excerpt: A federal judge is keeping East Potomac Park open for now, but hasn't ordered the government to keep the municipal golf course operational.
stories.lead:
Runners and cyclists still have access to D.C.'s East Potomac Park, despite the Trump administration's plans to close it over the weekend. But its golf course is conspicuously missing the flags that typically mark the holes — and at least some of the people who typically play them.

Federal Judge Ana Reyes issued a restraining order late Saturday to keep the beloved park open for two weeks, just hours before the National Park Service planned to cut off public access to most of it indefinitely.

stories.title: Who to watch in Spain's election race
stories.excerpt: Spain votes on 29 November, with the conservatives leading most polls after eight years of Socialist-led rule.
stories.lead:
Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.

He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.

Sánchez called the snap election eight months early, seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.

stories.title: Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda
stories.excerpt: Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's visit to Washington in September.
stories.lead:
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.

The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

stories.title: Energy bills forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as UK inflation rises again
stories.excerpt: Inflation is likely to keep rising on fresh forecasts that household energy bills will jump by 26% in January.
stories.lead:
Gas and electricity bills are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as energy costs continue to push up the UK's inflation rate.

The annual price cap on gas and elecrtricity is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to researchers at consultancy Cornwall Insight. Energy regulator Ofgem will announce the new cap next Wednesday, 25 November.

A sharp jump means inflation is at risk of continuing to rise - official data revealed prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices.
